summary.text: The Bohr model pictured the atom as a small dense nucleus with electrons orbiting it, like a solar system held together by electric attraction.
Niels Bohr built it between 1911 and 1918 on Rutherford's discovery of the nucleus, adding the rule that electron energies take only certain discrete values.
It is now obsolete, but it explained hydrogen's spectral lines and is still taught as a first step into quantum mechanics.

facts.value: Explained the Rydberg formula for hydrogen's spectral lines

facts.value: Electron energies assume only discrete values

facts.value: The quantum atomic model, in the 1920s

items.prompt: The Bohr atom looks like a mini solar system. What holds the electrons in orbit instead of gravity?

options.label: The electrostatic attraction to the nucleus
Magnetic tape around the nucleus
Friction with the surrounding air
Gravity from the nucleus alone

items.explain: The structure resembles the Solar System, but attraction comes from the electrostatic force, with electron energies quantized.

items.prompt: Hydrogen glows in sharp colored lines that people had measured and written as a formula. What did Bohr's model add?

options.label: A cheaper way to make hydrogen
Proof that hydrogen has no nucleus
A theoretical reason behind the formula's structure
A recipe for making brighter lamps

items.explain: The Rydberg formula was known experimentally, but only the Bohr model gave it a theoretical basis and explained its constants.

items.prompt: Thomson's plum pudding atom spread positive charge through a sphere. What result in 1908 troubled that picture?

options.label: Alpha particles sometimes bounced at large angles
Electrons were seen to be negative
Atoms turned out to be too heavy
Hydrogen glowed in too few colours

items.explain: Geiger and Marsden found alpha particles occasionally scatter at large angles, inconsistent with Thomson's model, which Rutherford explained with a compact center.

items.prompt: Classical physics says a circling electron should keep radiating energy. Why did that trouble early planetary atom models?

options.label: Orbiting electrons would turn into photons instantly
Orbits would be too perfectly circular
Electrons are always at rest in classical theory
A continuously accelerating electron would be mechanically unstable

items.explain: Larmor showed an accelerating charge radiates power, and electrons forced into orbit accelerate continuously, making them unstable.

items.prompt: If the Bohr model is obsolete, why do teachers still use it?

options.label: No better model is known
It is simple and right for some systems
It beats modern quantum mechanics
It was finally proved in 1925

items.explain: Because of its simplicity and correct results for some systems, it is used to introduce quantum mechanics and energy level diagrams.

items.prompt: Spectral lines come from differences between what quantities in Bohr's view?

options.label: Nucleus sizes
Electron colours
Orbit speeds
Atomic energy levels

items.explain: Bohr recognized the special frequencies called terms as energy levels divided by the Planck constant, so spectral lines come from energy differences.

paragraphs.heading: A planetary atom
paragraphs.text: The Bohr model, also called the Rutherford–Bohr model, is an outdated picture of the atom that brought in some early quantum ideas. It shows a small, dense nucleus with electrons orbiting around it. The layout resembles the Solar System, but electric attraction does the job that gravity does for planets. And the electrons may only have certain set energies, not any value at all: their energies are quantized.

paragraphs.heading: Where it came from
paragraphs.text: Niels Bohr developed the model between 1911 and 1918, building on Ernest Rutherford's discovery of the nucleus. It took over from Thomson's plum pudding model, and was itself replaced by the quantum atomic model in the 1920s. Compared with Rutherford's 1911 model, the main change was a new quantum interpretation taken from Haas and Nicholson. Bohr also gave up any attempt to explain radiation with classical physics.

paragraphs.heading: The problem to solve
paragraphs.text: In the late 1800s, some people imagined atoms as planetary systems with charged electrons in orbit. In 1897 Joseph Larmor showed, from classical electrodynamics, that an accelerating charge gives off power as radiation. An electron kept in orbit is always accelerating, so such an atom would be mechanically unstable. When Bohr started in 1912, Thomson's plum pudding model was the best available: rings of electrons inside a sphere of positive charge. But Thomson could not explain the many lines in atomic spectra.

paragraphs.heading: Rutherford's nucleus
paragraphs.text: In 1908 Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden showed that alpha particles sometimes scatter at large angles, which did not fit Thomson's model. In 1911 Rutherford explained this with a compact, highly charged mass at the atom's center. His scattering did not involve the electrons, so his picture of the atom was incomplete. Bohr opened his first paper by describing this atom: a small, dense, positive nucleus pulling on negative electrons.

paragraphs.heading: Explaining hydrogen's light
paragraphs.text: By the early 1900s, a good model of the atom was expected to account for its many spectral lines. Johann Balmer and Johannes Rydberg had summed these up in formulas drawn from measurements. The Bohr model's key success was explaining the Rydberg formula for the lines hydrogen gives off, which until then had no theory behind it. Another advance, the Rydberg–Ritz combination principle, tied line frequencies to differences between "terms", special frequencies typical of each element. Bohr read these terms as the atom's energy levels divided by the Planck constant. That led to the modern view that spectral lines come from differences in energy.

paragraphs.heading: Why it is still taught
paragraphs.text: Today the Bohr model counts as an obsolete theory. It can be obtained from quantum mechanics, which is broader and far more accurate, as a first-order approximation of the hydrogen atom. But it is simple and gives correct results for some systems. So it is still used to introduce students to quantum mechanics and to energy level diagrams.
